title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: How Play-Doh Works
summary: Josh and Chuck cover Play-Doh (spelled "Plato" in the transcript's auto-captions; hosts say Play-Doh in context) as part of the 12 Days of Christmas Toys playlist. They trace its origin from Cincinnati wallpaper-cleaning putty made by Joe McVicker's Kutol Products, through the 1950 non-toxic version with almond scent, the Captain Kangaroo promotion, the Rainbow Crafts Company and Pete the Kid mascot, the 1960 Fun Factory extruder, and current production and licensing. They then explain the chemistry: starch and water gelatinization, retrogradation, amylose/amylopectin ratios, mineral oil lubricant, surfactants, salt as preservative, and homemade recipes such as cream of tartar dough. Also covered: Play-Doh 3D printers, Singapore "scam ads," and a listener mail about sneaking into PG-13 movies to hear the one F-bomb.

segments.title: Opening banter and 12 Days of Christmas Toys intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as part of the 12 Days of Christmas Toys playlist. The hosts banter about voices, headphones, and SYSK T-shirts.

segments.title: Childhood memories of Play-Doh and its scent
segments.summary: The hosts recall eating or tasting Play-Doh paste as kids and the distinctive smell. Chuck mentions a 2006 fiftieth-anniversary scent perfume. They note Play-Doh was owned by Kenner and then Tonka before Hasbro.

segments.title: Origins: wallpaper cleaner from Joe McVicker's company
segments.summary: Joe McVicker's family soap company, Kutol Products, sold a gooey putty for cleaning coal soot and grease off wallpaper. When natural gas arrived sales fell, and McVicker's sister-in-law Kesu Fall suggested turning the putty into a toy after seeing kids make ornaments from it.

segments.title: 1950 launch and Captain Kangaroo deal
segments.summary: McVicker made a non-toxic version with almond scent in 1950 and donated cans to Cincinnati schools. He made a deal with Captain Kangaroo host Bob Keeshan for two percent of gross sales in exchange for on-air mentions, which Keeshan increased to up to three times a week.

segments.title: Rainbow Crafts, John Ruthven design, and Pete the Kid
segments.summary: The company formed Rainbow Crafts to separate from Kutol, and wildlife artist John Ruthven designed the first package. The mascot changed from an elf to Pete the Kid in a smock and beret, later replaced by a baseball cap in 2002 and a can-with-arms design.

segments.title: Modeling tips and cleaning Play-Doh from carpet
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that Play-Doh dries out when left out and is not meant to be permanent, unlike modeling clay. Hasbro's advice for carpet cleanup is to let it dry, brittle, and brush it out rather than use warm water.

segments.title: Fun Factory extruder and Play-Doh production stats
segments.summary: In 1960 General Electric engineers designed the Fun Factory, a hand-pushed lever extruder that forces dough through shaped holes. The hosts cite sales figures and a fact that all Play-Doh ever made would wrap the Earth about 300 times. Production is about 100 million cans a year.

segments.title: Licensing, fake food, and ingredients
segments.summary: The hosts discuss licensing deals such as Disney Princess sets and past Pizza Hut pizza ads, plus the sweet shop line. They note that gluten-free labeling matters because of wheat starch, and that the recipe is proprietary but the main ingredients are water, starch, and flour, with a patent cited.

segments.title: Full ingredient list and color history
segments.summary: Josh lists ingredients including starch binder, retrogradation inhibitor, salt, lubricant, surfactant, preservative, hardener, humectant, fragrance, and color. Salt was adjusted by a new chemist. The original colors were red, yellow, blue, and white, with more added in the eighties; the scent is said to be vanilla.

segments.title: Chemistry of starch: amylose and amylopectin
segments.summary: Chuck explains that Play-Doh's base is starch made of amylose (linear) and amylopectin (branched), forming starburst-shaped molecules held by hydrogen bonds around a hollow hilum. Hosts discuss the transition to chemistry as an interest.

segments.title: Gelatinization and retrogradation
segments.summary: Warm water or mechanical mixing gelatinizes starch into a gel, but excess amylose causes retrogradation, where it binds to itself and dries brittle. The formula uses about 25 percent amylose and 75 percent amylopectin as a balance.

segments.title: Lubricant, mineral oil, and surfactants
segments.summary: Too much amylopectin makes dough sticky, so a lubricant, likely mineral oil derived from petroleum, is added. A surfactant is needed to bind the lubricant and water so they stay mixed, with one hydrophilic end and one hydrophobic end.

segments.title: Drying, salt preservative, and manufacturing
segments.summary: Play-Doh dries from evaporation, and Hasbro suggests wrapping it in a damp paper towel. Salt is added for excess water and as an antimicrobial preservative. Ingredients are mixed with heat, packaged, and shelf life is considered.

segments.title: Making homemade Play-Doh recipes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss homemade recipes, with cream of tartar giving firmness, and suggest making it as a chemistry lesson for kids. Peanut butter Play-Doh recipes are mentioned.

segments.title: Play-Doh 3D printers and Singapore scam ads
segments.summary: Two Play-Doh 3D printers are mentioned, including a think Geek model and the Da Vinci. The hosts discuss a Singapore series of dark Play-Doh ads made without Hasbro's approval, and the concept of scam ads.

segments.title: Listener mail: sneaking into PG-13 movies and the one F-bomb
segments.summary: A listener from Kauai recounts sneaking into R-rated movies as a kid and counting swear words in PG-13 films, with the hosts discussing examples like Anchorman, Skyfall, Oblivion, Lincoln, and Philomena.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck invites listeners to contact the show by Twitter, Facebook, email, or the website, and the episode closes.
